title: The Housing Authority: vouchers funded, vouchers used, and the cost of each
question: How many rent vouchers is the San Francisco Housing Authority funded for, how many are in use, what does each cost the federal government, and what does the Authority spend on running the program?
finding: The federal housing department’s yearly file shows the Authority funded for 8,847 vouchers in 2015 and 16,111 in 2025. The share in use fell to 82% in 2022, leaving about 2,843 funded vouchers unused, and was 96% in 2025. Federal spending per voucher rose from $1,470 a month to $2,735 (86% more). The Authority’s own monthly reports show $440.8 million of housing assistance payments in 2025 against $331.4 million in 2022, and running costs of $23.9 million (5.4% of the payments). Its unrestricted reserve for the program was below zero in 48 of the 48 months reported, moving from minus $28.3 million in 2022-01 to minus $284,147 in 2025-12.
how: Vouchers funded, share in use, federal spending per voucher-month, the family’s own rent and months on the waiting list are the Housing Choice Voucher row for the San Francisco Housing Authority (code CA001) in the federal Picture of Subsidized Households, one snapshot each December, 2015 to 2025. Unused vouchers are funded vouchers times the share not in use. Housing assistance payments, vouchers under lease and administrative expenses are added up over the twelve monthly reports the Authority files in the federal Voucher Management System (2022 to 2025); the reserve is the December figure.
limits: The Housing Authority is a separate public body under federal rules, not a City department, and nothing here is a finding. An unused voucher is not money lost: unspent subsidy stays in reserve, and vouchers go unused when rents outrun the payment standard or units are being converted from public housing. Spending per voucher follows San Francisco rents. The two federal files count differently, so their voucher totals do not match exactly. The Authority’s notes to the monthly reports say the negative reserve includes accrued pension and retiree-health liabilities ($10.3 million as of September 2024).
